title: Models of neurons and networks
text:
13_02  MODELS OF NEURONS AND NETWORKS

Computational neuroscience is the attempt to explain the brain with mathematics precise enough to simulate. Its central tool is the model: a set of equations, usually differential equations, that captures some property of neurons or circuits while deliberately ignoring others. The art lies in choosing what to ignore. A model of a single sodium channel, a model of a cortical column, and a model of decision making in a whole animal need very different levels of detail. This section climbs a ladder of abstraction, from biophysical neurons to rate networks, and shows at each rung how the models relate to the artificial networks of machine learning.

THE MODELLING LADDER

Think of the levels as follows, from most detailed to most abstract:

1. Multi-compartment biophysical models: the neuron's morphology is divided into hundreds or thousands of cable segments (Chapter 5), each with Hodgkin-Huxley-type channels.
2. Single-compartment conductance models: one isopotential compartment with Hodgkin-Huxley equations.
3. Reduced spiking models: integrate-and-fire and its relatives, or two-variable models such as FitzHugh-Nagumo and Izhikevich.
4. Rate models: the neuron's output is a continuous firing rate.
5. Population or mean-field models: equations for the average activity of whole populations.
6. Normative and algorithmic models: what is being computed and why, with implementation left open (see 13_03).

David Marr, in his 1982 book Vision, distinguished computational, algorithmic and implementational levels of explanation. The ladder above is mostly about the implementational and algorithmic levels, but a good model connects all three.

BIOPHYSICAL MODELS

Chapter 5 presented the Hodgkin-Huxley equations and cable theory. Combining them gives the compartmental model. For compartment j with neighbours k, the voltage obeys

  C_j dV_j/dt = - sum over channels of g_c(V_j, t) (V_j - E_c) + sum over k of g_jk (V_k - V_j) + I_syn,j

where g_jk is the axial coupling conductance between compartments. Simulators such as NEURON, developed by Michael Hines and Ted Carnevale, solve these equations efficiently for complex morphologies. Such models explain phenomena that simpler models cannot: dendritic spikes, backpropagating action potentials, and the way the location of a synapse affects its influence. Work by Bartlett Mel, Michael Hausser and others argued that a single pyramidal neuron with active dendrites can behave like a two-layer network of nonlinear subunits. In 2021 David Beniaguev, Idan Segev and Michael London reported in Neuron that a temporally convolutional deep network with several layers was needed to reproduce the input-output behaviour of a detailed model of a cortical layer 5 pyramidal neuron, largely because of NMDA-receptor-dependent dendritic nonlinearities. In other words, one biological neuron may be computationally richer than one artificial neuron by a large factor.

The most ambitious biophysical project was the Blue Brain Project at EPFL, led by Henry Markram, which published in Cell in 2015 a reconstruction and simulation of a piece of juvenile rat somatosensory cortex with around 31,000 neurons. It was valuable as a data integration effort and simulation platform, but also criticised for the difficulty of drawing functional conclusions from a model with so many parameters. The tension between detail and understanding is permanent in this field.

INTEGRATE-AND-FIRE MODELS

The most widely used reduced model predates Hodgkin and Huxley. Louis Lapicque in 1907 modelled the nerve membrane as a capacitor charging through a resistance, with excitation when the voltage reached a threshold. The modern leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron is

  tau_m dV/dt = - (V - E_L) + R_m I(t)

  if V >= V_th: emit a spike, set V = V_reset, hold for a refractory period t_ref

where tau_m = R_m C_m is the membrane time constant, usually 10 to 30 ms. Between spikes, it is a linear low-pass filter, the RC circuit of any electronics course. The spike itself is not modelled; it is an event.

For a constant current I above threshold, the time to reach threshold from reset can be solved exactly, giving the firing rate

  r = 1 / ( t_ref + tau_m ln( (R_m I + E_L - V_reset) / (R_m I + E_L - V_th) ) )

which is zero below a threshold current and rises, roughly linearly at high currents, saturating at 1/t_ref. This f-I curve (firing rate versus input current) is the biological origin of the activation function.

Extensions add realism at small cost. The exponential integrate-and-fire model of Nicolas Fourcaud-Trocme, Nicolas Brunel and colleagues adds a term Delta_T exp((V - V_T)/Delta_T) to capture spike initiation sharpness. The adaptive exponential model (AdEx) of Romain Brette and Wulfram Gerstner (2005) adds an adaptation current w:

  C dV/dt = - g_L (V - E_L) + g_L Delta_T exp((V - V_T)/Delta_T) - w + I
  tau_w dw/dt = a (V - E_L) - w
  on spike: V -> V_reset, w -> w + b

With different parameters, AdEx reproduces regular spiking, bursting, adaptation and fast spiking. Eugene Izhikevich's 2003 model achieves similar variety with two quadratic equations:

  dv/dt = 0.04 v^2 + 5 v + 140 - u + I
  du/dt = a (b v - u)
  if v >= 30 mV: v -> c, u -> u + d

where the four parameters a, b, c, d select firing patterns. It is cheap enough to simulate very large networks.

TWO-DIMENSIONAL INSIGHT: PHASE PLANES

FitzHugh in 1961, and Nagumo and colleagues with an electronic circuit in 1962, reduced Hodgkin-Huxley to two variables: a fast voltage-like variable v and a slow recovery variable w.

  dv/dt = v - v^3/3 - w + I
  dw/dt = epsilon (v + a - b w)

This allows phase-plane analysis. Plot the nullclines, where dv/dt = 0 (a cubic) and dw/dt = 0 (a line). Their intersection is the resting state. As I increases, the fixed point loses stability and a limit cycle, repetitive spiking, appears. The type of bifurcation determines the neuron's computational character. John Rinzel and Bard Ermentrout clarified this classification: neurons of Hodgkin's "class 1" can fire at arbitrarily low rates (a saddle-node on invariant circle bifurcation), while "class 2" neurons start firing at a non-zero rate (a Hopf bifurcation) and tend to resonate at preferred frequencies. Engineers recognise this as nonlinear dynamics and control theory applied to cells.

RATE MODELS AND NETWORKS

Averaging over spikes gives rate models. For a population of neurons with rates r_i,

  tau dr_i/dt = - r_i + f( sum over j of W_ij r_j + I_i )

where f is the f-I curve, often a sigmoid or rectified linear function. Hugh Wilson and Jack Cowan in 1972 wrote coupled equations for excitatory and inhibitory populations, producing oscillations and multistability, the ancestor of many models of cortical rhythms. Shun-ichi Amari analysed neural field equations in which populations are arranged in space, producing bumps of activity.

Notice how close this equation is to a recurrent neural network in machine learning. Discretise in time with step dt and set alpha = dt/tau:

  r(t+1) = (1 - alpha) r(t) + alpha f( W r(t) + I(t) )

This is a "leaky" RNN, and with alpha = 1 it is the vanilla RNN, h(t+1) = f(W h(t) + U x(t)).

ATTRACTOR NETWORKS

John Hopfield in 1982 described a network of binary units with symmetric connections W_ij = W_ji and an energy function

  E = - (1/2) sum over i,j of W_ij s_i s_j

that decreases with each asynchronous update. Memories are stored as minima of the energy by a Hebbian rule, W_ij proportional to the sum over patterns of x_i x_j, and recall is descent to the nearest minimum from a partial cue. Chapter 9 described its role in memory theory. Attractor networks also model working memory, where persistent activity maintains information after a stimulus disappears, and continuous variables such as head direction or position, via ring or sheet attractors whose activity bump can move along a continuum of stable states. In 2017 Seung Wook Kim, Vivek Jayaraman and colleagues reported in Science that the fly's head direction system has the ring-attractor dynamics such models predicted. Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for foundational discoveries enabling machine learning with artificial neural networks.

BALANCED NETWORKS

Why are cortical neurons so irregular, with Poisson-like firing (13_01), when integrate-and-fire neurons driven by constant input fire like clocks? Carl van Vreeswijk and Haim Sompolinsky proposed in 1996 that in networks with strong excitatory and inhibitory connections, large excitation and inhibition approximately cancel, leaving fluctuations that drive irregular, chaotic firing. This "balanced state" arises naturally in randomly connected networks and explains asynchronous irregular activity. Measurements of excitatory and inhibitory currents in cortex supported the idea that they are often closely balanced. Nicolas Brunel in 2000 mapped the states of sparse networks of integrate-and-fire neurons: synchronous or asynchronous, regular or irregular, depending on the balance and input.

Haim Sompolinsky, Andrea Crisanti and Hans-Jurgen Sommers showed in 1988 that random rate networks with strong enough coupling become chaotic. This matters for machine learning: the transition from ordered to chaotic dynamics relates to vanishing and exploding gradients, and initialising networks near the "edge of chaos" was later shown to help train deep networks.

RESERVOIRS AND TRAINED RECURRENT NETWORKS

If a random recurrent network has rich dynamics, perhaps one only needs to train a readout. Herbert Jaeger's echo state networks (2001) and Wolfgang Maass, Thomas Natschlager and Henry Markram's liquid state machines (2002) did exactly that: a fixed random reservoir, a trained linear output. David Sussillo and Larry Abbott in 2009 introduced FORCE learning to train chaotic rate networks to produce complex outputs by feeding the output back and rapidly modifying weights with recursive least squares.

A powerful approach then emerged: train an RNN on the same task an animal performs, and compare its internal dynamics with neural recordings. In 2013 Valerio Mante, David Sussillo, Krishna Shenoy and William Newsome reported in Nature that an RNN trained on a context-dependent decision task reproduced features of prefrontal population activity in monkeys, and analysis of the trained network's fixed points revealed a mechanism for selecting the relevant input. David Sussillo and Omri Barak introduced methods for finding fixed points and linearising RNN dynamics around them, turning "black box" networks into analysable dynamical systems. Such task-trained networks are now a standard hypothesis-generating tool, closely related to the task-optimised CNNs of Chapter 8.

SIMULATING SPIKING NETWORKS AND TRAINING THEM

Simulators like NEST, Brian (in Python) and NEURON allow networks of spiking neurons at scales from hundreds to millions of cells. Training spiking networks with gradient descent is harder than training rate networks because the spike is a discontinuous step: its derivative is zero almost everywhere and infinite at threshold. The surrogate gradient method, reviewed by Emre Neftci, Hesham Mostafa and Friedemann Zenke in 2019, replaces the derivative of the step with a smooth function, such as the derivative of a fast sigmoid, during the backward pass only. Combined with backpropagation through time, this allows spiking networks to be trained on tasks like speech recognition with competitive accuracy. It is a pragmatic trick: forward pass with true spikes, backward pass with a smoothed proxy. Biologically plausible alternatives such as e-prop (Guillaume Bellec, Maass and colleagues, 2020) approximate the gradient with local eligibility traces and a broadcast learning signal, a three-factor rule (Chapter 7).

CONNECTIONS TO AI AND MACHINE LEARNING

1. Same equations, different goals. The rate equation and the RNN are the same mathematical object. The neuroscientist asks whether the dynamics resemble the brain; the ML engineer asks whether the network performs the task. Task-trained RNNs merge both questions.

2. How powerful is a neuron? Detailed models suggest single neurons with active dendrites compute functions requiring multi-layer artificial networks. Some ML research explores dendrite-inspired units, with multiple nonlinear branches, but standard deep learning has thrived with simple point units, scaling the number instead.

3. Dynamics and trainability. Chaos theory of random networks and the edge-of-chaos initialisation in deep learning are the same mathematics. Gated RNNs like LSTMs control the effective time constant of each unit, like the tau in the leaky rate equation; modern state-space sequence models (for example S4 and Mamba) can be seen as carefully parameterised linear dynamical systems with nonlinear readouts, a design close in spirit to the linear filter plus nonlinearity models of neuroscience.

4. Energy and attractors. Hopfield's energy function anticipated energy-based models and Boltzmann machines. Hubert Ramsauer, Sepp Hochreiter and colleagues showed in 2020 that modern continuous Hopfield networks with an exponential energy have an update rule equivalent to transformer attention (Chapter 9).

5. Spiking networks. Surrogate gradients brought deep learning to spiking models, enabling neuromorphic hardware applications (13_04).

SUMMARY

Models range from detailed compartmental neurons to abstract rate networks. Integrate-and-fire neurons capture spiking with an RC circuit and a threshold; phase-plane analysis explains firing types; rate equations become RNNs; Hopfield networks show memory as attractors; balanced networks explain irregular firing; and trained RNNs reveal mechanisms comparable to recorded brain dynamics. Throughout, computational neuroscience and machine learning use the same equations, and progress in one increasingly comes from the other.
